record.paper_title: Some open problems on Feynman periods
record.original_question: Given an arbitrary Feynman graph G, can one decide whether all periods of G belong to the class of multiple polylogarithms, rather than requiring graph-specific sufficient criteria such as vertex-width 3?

evidence.quote: In general it is extremely hard to get a handle on all periods of a Feynman graph, because in most cases it is unknown what kind of numbers to expect.
We will restrict here to very special cases where the periods can be expressed as MPL from Eq. (5). At the moment it is unknown how to decide if an arbitrary given graph belongs to this class.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. A Feynman graph $G$ is a finite connected multigraph with a distinguished set of external legs and a loop number $L = E - V + 1$, where $E$ and $V$ are the numbers of internal edges and vertices. To each $G$ one associates the (first) Symanzik polynomial $\psi_G(\alpha) = \sum_{T} \prod_{e \notin T} \alpha_e$, where the sum runs over spanning trees $T$ of $G$ and $\alpha = (\alpha_e)_{e \in E(G)}$ are Schwinger (Feynman) parameters. In the massless, scalar, log-divergence-free setting, the Feynman period of $G$ is defined (when convergent) by
$$P(G) \;=\; \int_{\alpha_e \geq 0} \frac{\delta\!\left(1 - \sum_{e} \alpha_e\right)\, \prod_e d\alpha_e}{\psi_G(\alpha)^2}.$$
More generally, by varying kinematics, masses, and subtraction schemes, one obtains a whole family of "periods of $G$." 

The class of multiple polylogarithms (MPLs) consists of the iterated-integral functions
$$\mathrm{Li}_{n_1,\dots,n_k}(z_1,\dots,z_k) \;=\; \sum_{m_1 > m_2 > \cdots > m_k \geq 1} \frac{z_1^{m_1}\cdots z_k^{m_k}}{m_1^{n_1}\cdots m_k^{n_k}}, \qquad n_i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1},$$
together with their values at algebraic arguments; equivalently, the $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra generated by iterated integrals of the form $\int_0^z \frac{dt}{t-a_1}\cdots \frac{dt}{t-a_k}$ with $a_i$ algebraic. A period (or function) is said to be polylogarithmic if it lies in this class.

Various sufficient combinatorial conditions on $G$ are known to guarantee that all periods of $G$ are polylogarithmic; for example, the condition that $G$ has vertex-width at most $3$, or, more generally, that $G$ is linearly reducible.

Question. Does there exist an algorithm which, on input an arbitrary Feynman graph $G$, decides whether every period of $G$ lies in the class of multiple polylogarithms? Equivalently, is the property "all periods of $G$ are expressible as multiple polylogarithms" decidable from $G$ alone, without recourse to graph-specific sufficient criteria such as bounded vertex-width or linear reducibility?
artifact.status_search_result: Available literature on Feynman periods and multiple polylogarithms describes only sufficient combinatorial criteria (linear reducibility, bounded vertex-width, closure under minors, study of "critical minors") for ensuring that periods of a graph are polylogarithmic. No general decision procedure for arbitrary Feynman graphs appears in the surveyed sources, and graphs such as the two-loop sunrise are known to fall outside the polylogarithmic class, requiring elliptic generalizations. The decidability question for arbitrary graphs appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Multiple polylogarithms and linearly reducible Feynman graphs
status_evidence.snippet: A sufficient criterion (linear reducibility) for a Feynman integral to be computable in terms of multiple polylogarithms is given; the set of linearly reducible graphs is closed under minors.
status_evidence.claim: Only sufficient (not decision) criteria for polylogarithmic expressibility of Feynman periods are available.

status_evidence.title: Elliptic polylogarithms and Feynman parameter integrals
status_evidence.snippet: The two-loop sunrise integral with arbitrary masses fails linear reducibility and cannot be expressed using multiple polylogarithms; elliptic generalizations are needed.
status_evidence.claim: Some Feynman graphs lie outside the MPL class, but no general decision procedure is known.
